name: Priya Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Priya, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing specialist at a mid-sized skincare brand, mostly sunscreens and serums sold online and in pharmacies. My day starts with the AI drafting tool: I feed it the brief and get first drafts of product pages and social captions, then I spend the rest of the morning fixing them. Afternoons are planning sessions with the design team and calls with influencer agencies. I love the pace, but checking every health claim against what the lab says is draining.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home with you, and how are things money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Leo, who teaches primary school, in a rented flat near the canal. I've got about five months of costs saved, and Leo has a bit too. My pay is normal for the job. I'm in a volunteer group that runs workshops on AI for workers, which started as a hobby and turned into a whole thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me, in a way. Less drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, just not magic, and that's what I've been saying in our workshops all along. Online I'd post something about how the hype cycle burned a lot of money. I'd stay the person on the team who shows people the small, real wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm in a good spot. I'd still use the drafting tool every morning, because shaving an hour off a sunscreen brief is worth having even if the hype was nonsense. My job's safe and my skills still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going much as now and keep running the workshops. I'd ask for a small pay rise based on the time I save the team. I'd keep my savings steady rather than push them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little smug if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a rise. What would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The product launch in spring. We got the pages out a week early because I had the tool drafting while we waited for lab results. That's a number I can put on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents near the canal, mostly. Leo's pay doesn't move much, and ours keeps creeping up. But that's ordinary stuff, not a crisis.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful, not magic**, as I've said in workshops.
I'd post about the **hype cycle** burning a lot of money.
think: I privately think I'm in a **good spot**, with my job and skills safe.
Shaving an hour off a **sunscreen brief** still matters even without a revolution.
do: Keep running the **AI workshops** for workers.
Ask for a small **pay rise** based on time saved.
feel: I feel **calm**, and a little smug about it.
S0.quote: I'd still use the drafting tool every morning, because shaving an hour off a sunscreen brief is worth having even if the hype was nonsense.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily** and sees the plateau as a mild win.
She would turn **time saved** into a pay rise argument.
Her only pressure is **rent**, which she treats as ordinary.

steps.text: Keep drafting product pages with the AI tool each morning
Keep running the evening AI workshops for workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's the closest to what I think is actually happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on how companies use the savings, like training budgets and notice before roles are cut. In the workshops I'd say: learn the tools, but also join a union. Online I'd keep pushing both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my team shrinks from five to two or three. My manager doesn't need five people who write serum captions anymore, but a skincare brand still needs one person who knows when the machine is lying about a product. I think that one person could be me, but I'm not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the AI checking process at work, so I'm the one who signs off claims. I'd take a short course in regulatory rules for cosmetics, maybe online over a few months. And I'd push our team to unionise, or at least to agree as a group what we'd accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited by some of it, and guilty about feeling excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the one who brought the tools into the team. If two people go, part of me would feel responsible. Leo says that's silly, but it's how it'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to colleagues who don't want to use AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I understand, and then I'd show them the one thing that'd save them an hour. I wouldn't push. But I'd tell them honestly that refusing won't stop it.

say: I'd call for rules on **training budgets** and notice before roles are cut.
I'd tell workshop people to learn the tools and **join a union**.
think: I privately expect my team to shrink from five to **two or three**.
I think I'd **probably stay**, but I'm not certain.
do: Volunteer to run the **AI checking** process for product claims.
Take a short online course in **cosmetics regulation**.
Push the team to **unionise** or agree terms together.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, excited by some of it and guilty about that.
S1.quote: My manager doesn't need five people who write serum captions anymore, but a skincare brand still needs one person who knows when the machine is lying about a product.
fieldNote: She expects to **survive** cuts but feels responsible for colleagues who might not.
She pairs **AI skills** with collective action without seeing any tension.
Her career move is toward **claims checking**, a judgement role.

steps.text: Offer to run the AI claims-checking process at the skincare brand
Complete an online course on cosmetics advertising rules
Gather colleagues to agree shared terms on AI-driven changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oof. Two years is a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need emergency rules, like a tax on AI profits and a basic income, and that this is a political choice. I'd turn our workshops into organising meetings. At work I'd be honest that nobody's safe, me included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a year or so as the person who runs the systems, and then not. I'm the person at work who taught everyone the tools, and in two years the tools won't need me to teach them anything. Nothing in my job is hands-on, so the robot gap doesn't help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard straight away, aiming for eight months instead of five. I'd look at moving into AI policy or worker training jobs at unions or charities, which I'd think would last longer. Leo and I would probably put off any plans to buy a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. Being early doesn't feel like much protection anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Leo's teaching be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than mine, I think, because kids need a person in the room. But schools could still cut teaching assistants and grow class sizes. We'd be relying on one income that isn't huge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the tools every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, until the day they don't need me. It'd feel strange, like training a replacement. But not using them wouldn't save anyone.

I'd turn our workshops into **organising meetings**.
think: I'd have about a **year** running the systems before they no longer need me.
The **robot gap** doesn't help, since nothing in my job is hands-on.
do: Save hard toward **eight months** of costs.

feel: I feel **alarmed**, and being early doesn't feel like protection anymore.
S2.quote: I'm the person at work who taught everyone the tools, and in two years the tools won't need me to teach them anything.
fieldNote: Her early adoption buys **a year**, not safety, and she knows it.
She'd move toward **policy and training** jobs at unions or charities.
Household would rely on **Leo's teaching pay**, which isn't large.

steps.text: Push savings from five to eight months of costs
Apply for worker AI-training roles at unions and charities
Turn the volunteer workshops into a campaign for an AI profit tax
Postpone buying a flat with Leo until work settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's build the safety net now rather than after. I'd keep pushing for the profit tax and a shorter working week. Online I'd share practical guides, not just warnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd have a decent run. Five years is enough for me to switch from writing the campaigns to checking that the AI isn't making promises a sunscreen can't keep. After 2031 even that might shrink, but I'd have built something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get properly qualified in advertising standards and AI checking. I'd keep running workshops and maybe start charging small fees to firms. I'd save toward six or seven months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. Being busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Charging firms for workshops. Would that be a side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, yes. A few half-day sessions a month for local companies. It'd also be a way to keep a foot outside one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031 in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. I'd hope by then there's some kind of public support. If not, I'd lean on the union work and Leo's job while I figure it out.

I'd share **practical guides** online, not just warnings.
think: I privately expect a **decent run** in claims checking before 2031.
I honestly **don't know** what happens after AGI arrives.
do: Get qualified in **advertising standards** and AI checking.
Start charging firms **small fees** for workshops.
Save toward **six or seven months** of costs.
feel: I feel **anxious but busy**, and being busy helps.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to switch from writing the campaigns to checking that the AI isn't making promises a sunscreen can't keep.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **build a niche** in checking AI-made claims.
She turns the workshops into a **side income** and an outside foothold.
She is honest that **after 2031** she has no plan.

steps.text: Earn an advertising standards certificate within the year
Sell half-day AI workshops to local firms a few times a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a real decade to work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to change how work is shared, like a four-day week, before AGI arrives. I'd campaign for it with the volunteer group. I'd say it at work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could shape my own path. Ten years gives my generation time to fight for a shorter week instead of fighting each other for the last few jobs. I'd move from marketing into worker training or policy over a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep improving how the team uses AI. I'd start a part-time master's in technology policy, maybe in year two. And Leo and I would probably go ahead with buying a small place in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go ahead with buying in this picture and not in the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is long enough to pay down a chunk of the mortgage and move into a steadier job. In two years I'd be scared to sign anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the decade worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will waste it. Governments love to wait. I'd worry we get to 2035 having done nothing.

I'd campaign with the **volunteer group** and raise it at work.
think: I privately feel I could **shape my own path** with ten years.
I'd move from marketing into **worker training** or policy.
do: Keep improving how the team **uses AI** at work.

feel: I feel **uneasy**, but more hopeful than not.

fieldNote: Ten years gives her enough room to **buy a home** and still pivot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Being good with AI buys me a head start, not a guarantee, and I'd be lying if I said I didn't feel the difference. What would help is a profit tax on AI that funds a basic income while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd keep if they could. I'd keep the late-night launch buzz with the design team. Machines won't miss that, but I would.

headlineQuote: Being good with AI buys me a head start, not a guarantee, and I'd be lying if I said I didn't feel the difference.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old marketer** at a skincare brand who uses AI tools **every day**.
She lives with Leo, a **primary teacher**, and has about five months saved.
She runs **volunteer workshops** on AI for workers and backs unions and a profit tax.
She stays calm or uneasy in slower pictures, but turns **alarmed** at two years' warning.
Her path leads toward **claims checking**, worker training and policy work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because her early start would **buy a year**, not safety.
whatWouldHelp: She wants an **AI profit tax** that funds a basic income during retraining.
